findings.summary: The part teaches fan-out and fan-in (syllabus chapters 8–9) before the closing rules, `select`, and nil-channel semantics (chapters 5–7) that those patterns are built out of, inverting every prerequisite.
findings.evidence: Page 1 already uses `close(jobs) // all N range loops exit` and `case <-ctx.Done(): return // no leak`, but page 3 only later states "THE RULE: only a sender closes, and only if it is solo" and page 4 only later introduces "select waits on many channel operations at once" under the heading "select In One Screen".
findings.fix: Reorder the five pages to follow the syllabus: closing rules + panic/block tables, then `select`, then nil channels, then fan-out, then fan-in, then the leak/cheat-sheet page — so every construct a pattern page uses has already been defined.

findings.summary: The caption's body is copied from Part 1 and lists Part 1's topics, describing none of the five pages actually in Part 2.
findings.evidence: Part 2 caption: "unbuffered rendezvous, buffer sizing that is a memory ceiling rather than a perf knob, the hchan fast path, the three ways close panics, and the nil-channel trick" — these match Part 1's page_titles ("Unbuffered Channels: Rendezvous", "Buffered Channels: Sizing The Queue", "Inside The Runtime: hchan", "Closing Channels"), and parts/01/post.json carries the identical sentence verbatim. Part 2's pages are Fan-Out, Fan-In, Merge Leaks And Who Closes, Channel Or Mutex And select, nil Channels And The Decision Guide.
findings.fix: Rewrite the middle sentence around Part 2's actual content, e.g. "These five pages are the pattern layer: fan-out and picking N, the general fan-in merge, the two goroutine leaks and the who-closes rule, channel vs mutex, and nil channels as an off switch."

findings.summary: The caption claims ten pages but the carousel has five.
findings.evidence: "These ten pages are the whole channel model" vs. five entries in slides[] (Fan-Out, Fan-In, Merge Leaks And Who Closes, Channel Or Mutex And select, nil Channels And The Decision Guide).
findings.fix: Change "These ten pages" to "These five pages".

findings.summary: The first sentence is a bare series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: First sentence: "Part 2 of GO CHANNELS: FIELD NOTES." The hook — "Most Go concurrency bugs are not race conditions — they are one goroutine parked forever on a send nobody will ever receive." — is second; Part 1's caption leads with that same line.
findings.fix: Lead with a Part 2-specific hook and move the part label to the end, e.g. "Your worker pool did not crash — it is five goroutines all blocked on a send the consumer stopped reading. ... Part 2 of GO CHANNELS: FIELD NOTES."

findings.summary: The fan-in page calls the `wg.Wait()` closer goroutine "mandatory" but shows neither the producer goroutines nor the closer code, which only appears on the next page.

findings.fix: Put the `go func(){ wg.Wait(); close(out) }()` block on page 2 directly under the merge scaffold so the canonical merge is complete where it is claimed, and keep page 3 for the who-closes rule only.

findings.summary: The "Timer Leak" callout states outdated pre-Go 1.23 timer behaviour as current fact.
findings.evidence: "`case <-time.After(2*time.Second)` leaks its timer until it fires. In a hot loop use `time.NewTimer` with `defer t.Stop()` instead."
findings.fix: Qualify the version: "Before Go 1.23, `time.After` kept its timer alive until it fired; in a hot loop that is real garbage. Since Go 1.23 (modules declaring `go 1.23`+) an unreferenced timer is collectable immediately even without `Stop`, so `time.After` no longer leaks — `time.NewTimer` + `defer t.Stop()` is now about reuse and avoiding an allocation per iteration, not about leaks."

findings.summary: Page 4 opens with three stranded bullets about closing semantics that belong to page 3's closing section, arriving after the close panic table has already been taught.
findings.evidence: Page 4 begins with no heading: "Buffered values survive a close; receivers drain first","Closing wakes every goroutine blocked on receive","That broadcast is how one `done` cancels N workers" — then immediately switches to the heading "Channel Or Mutex".
findings.fix: Move those three bullets onto page 3 under the "Who Closes" heading, next to the panic/block table, and start page 4 with its own "Channel Or Mutex" heading.

findings.summary: Page 4 gives the nil-out fix for the closed-channel busy spin before the bug it fixes is ever described, which happens on page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ends with "if !ok { a = nil; continue }","// loop while a != nil || b != nil"; page 5 then opens with the symptom: "A closed input stays ready and busy-spins the loop","Nil the variable and select drops that case for good".
findings.fix: Move the two busy-spin bullets from the top of page 5 to page 4 immediately before the `if !ok { a = nil; continue }` block, so the bug is stated, then the fix shown.

findings.summary: The caption says close panics in three ways, but close itself panics in only two.
findings.evidence: caption: "the three ways close panics"; the deck's own table on page 3 lists close as panicking on exactly two states — "close | panic | panic" (on closed, on nil) — the third panic being `send` on a closed channel.
findings.fix: Reword to "the two ways `close` panics plus the send that panics on a closed channel" (or "the three channel panics").

findings.fix: Move the pipeline diagram to the end of page 2, after the fan-in definition and pipeline contract, where every node it names has been introduced.
